findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled when the request ends
findings.body: Each background legacy write (Create here, and likewise Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163) builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which is right after the goroutine is started. The legacy write will therefore often fail with `context canceled` or never complete, so legacy storage silently drifts from unified storage. That defeats the stated 'safe measure'. Detach the context, e.g. `context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...)`.

findings.title: Legacy write errors in the background goroutines are never logged
findings.body: The async goroutines in Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection only feed the error into a duration metric (an error boolean). They never log it or include the object, name or cause. The old code logged legacy failures. Now a failed legacy write leaves no trace in the logs, so divergence between the two stores is very hard to diagnose.

findings.title: Storage failure is recorded as a legacy duration in Create
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. The same mistake is in Update at line 129. As a result, unified-storage errors show up in the legacy-storage metrics and are missing from the storage error metrics, which makes the dashboards misleading.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded as a storage duration
findings.body: The background goroutine times `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` but records it with `d.recordStorageDuration`. Legacy latency and errors are therefore counted as unified-storage metrics, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection.

findings.title: Delete records the object name as the metric 'kind' label
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This puts per-object names into the kind label, producing unbounded Prometheus label cardinality and wrong kind attribution.

findings.title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the `name`, `kind` and `method` values that were just added to `log`. Every other method uses `log`, so storage/legacy code that logs from the context during Delete loses that context.

findings.title: Legacy Update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object stored in unified storage
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo in `updateWrapper` with the object returned by Storage.Update, so legacy received the same final object. Now legacy gets the raw `objInfo` and computes the update against its own (possibly divergent) current state. Patches or apply operations can therefore produce a different result in legacy than in unified storage, or fail. This also re-invokes objInfo asynchronously after the request has completed.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests share one mock for both stores and never verify the async legacy write
findings.body: `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` are built on the same `mock.Mock`, so an expectation such as `Create` or `Delete` is satisfied by either store. The tests cannot tell which store was called, and in Delete/DeleteCollection they set up only storage expectations. The tests never wait for or assert the background legacy call, so the core mode-3 behavior (legacy is written asynchronously after unified storage) is untested. The goroutine may also still be calling the mock after the test returns. Case names like 'creating an object only in the unified store' do not reflect what is actually verified.
